# On the Peculiar Comfort of Unfinished Things

I've been thinking about how we're all walking around with incomplete thoughts, half-read books, projects we swear we'll return to. There's something oddly honest about this state of incompleteness.

We treat it like a failure usually—the novel gathering dust, the hobby abandoned, the conversation we meant to have but didn't. Self-help culture tells us to finish what we start, to be disciplined, to cross things off. And sure, there's value in that. But I wonder if we're missing something by always treating "unfinished" as a synonym for "failed."

An unfinished book means I get to live in the possibility of what happens next. A half-learned skill means I haven't yet discovered I'm not good at it. A relationship with someone you've lost touch with exists in this strange quantum state—you didn't break it, it just... paused. Maybe that's gentler than a clean ending.

I think about how every conversation I have is technically unfinished. You never know what someone will remember from what you said. The impact ripples forward in ways you'll never see. In that sense, everything that matters is unfinished.

Maybe the real skill isn't completion. Maybe it's being okay with reaching a point of *enough*, and then moving on to the next incomplete thing. Enough presence, enough effort, enough care—and then releasing it.

There's freedom in that, somehow.
